rv.q: Yet it's not enough to detract from the overall triumph.
This show will touch a deep chord in everybody.
Visually, however, it is inspired, and never more so than when flashing fishy shapes in a watery wilderness assemble to create the ghostly face of Mufasa to remind Simba to avenge his death.
It lights up the West End with the blaze of Taymor's fabulous imagination.
The kaleidoscopic visual brilliance of Julie Taymor's production lies the ultimate source of the show's success.
Taymor’s vision for the piece remains a great and lasting one that should find Britons fighting for a glimpse of Pride Rock no less avidly than their Broadway brethren.
Julie Taymor's staging and costume design remains some of the most innovative, impressive and breath-taking to ever be seen on stage - musical or otherwise.
'The Lion King' is undoubtedly in a different league and children will be roaring their approval for a long time to come.
'The Lion King' is a show that demands to be seen.
But as blockbuster musicals go, this is one with beauty and brains.
It is spectacular and it is art; not, perhaps, the art of the Turner Prize, for it is far more beautiful than an unmade bed and has more vitality than a photograph of a washing-machine.
The Lion King isn’t a showstopping musical or a show to split sides or change minds, but it’s a decent evening of entertainment… especially if you’ve just finished your SATs.
Disney uses traditional African dress, dance and music styles as well as other techniques from around the world to bring these animals to life in a way that just somehow works.
So is The Lion King as good as they say it is? The answer is - dammit - yes.

PLAYHOUSE, EDINBURGH IF THIS winter’s chill is getting to you – and your heart feels sore and cold – it’s hard to imagine a better instant remedy than a visit to the Playhouse, where the current radiant UK stage production of Disney’s The Lion King is settling in for a three-and-a-half-month stay.
